procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Judicature at Bombay
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 12.02.2018 of the High Court of Judicature at Bombay in CRWP No. 5190 of 2017
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court dismissed the petition filed u/s.482 of CrPC for quashing FIR registered u/ss.376, 420, 504 and 506 IPC holding, inter alia, that the offence under Section 376 of IPC is an offence against the society which would require further investigation into the matter and does not warrant interference.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court allowed the appeal.

directions: The impugned judgement and order dated 12.02.2018 passed by the Bombay High Court in Criminal Writ Petition (CRWP) No. 5190 of 2017 is set aside.

The FIR being CR No. 302 of 2017 dated 15.08.2017 registered against the appellant with the Kharghar Police Station, Navi Mumbai under Sections 376, 420, 504 and 506 of the Indian Penal Code is quashed.
Quashing the FIR against the appellant will not be a bar to respondent no. 2 to seek any other remedy available under the law.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the petition filed under Section 482 of the CrPC for quashing the FIR registered against the appellant for offences under Sections 376, 420, 504, and 506 of the IPC.

facts: A complaint was filed alleging that the appellant, from 2008 to 2017, engaged in sexual intercourse with the complainant on the false promise of marriage, promising to deposit money and buy her a house.
An FIR was registered against the appellant for offences under Sections 376 (rape), 420 (cheating), 504 (intentional insult), and 506 (criminal intimidation) of the IPC.
The appellant filed a petition under Section 482 of the CrPC in the High Court to quash the FIR.
The High Court dismissed the petition, reasoning that an offence under Section 376 IPC is an offence against society that requires investigation and does not warrant interference.
law: Section 482 of the CrPC grants High Courts inherent power to pass orders to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or to secure the ends of justice.
When considering a petition to quash an FIR under this section, the court must take a prima facie view of the matter based on the materials on record.
If the factual allegations, taken at face value, do not make out a prima facie case for the commission of any offence, the High Court has the power to quash the FIR.
application: The Supreme Court examined the allegations in the FIR to determine if a prima facie case was made out.
It found that the facts and circumstances did not establish a prima facie case for the commission of rape under Section 376 IPC.

Furthermore, the Court noted that the FIR contained no allegations that would constitute the offences of cheating (Section 420), intentional insult (Section 504), or criminal intimidation (Section 506).

The Court reasoned that allowing the criminal proceedings to continue against the appellant, when no criminal liability could be attached based on the complaint, would amount to an abuse of the process of the court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision. It concluded that since the allegations in the FIR did not make out a prima facie case for any of the charged offences, continuing the criminal proceedings would be an abuse of the court's process. Therefore, the Supreme Court found the High Court was not justified in dismissing the petition, allowed the appeal, and quashed the FIR.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in dismissing the petition filed under Section 482 of the CrPC for quashing the FIR registered against the appellant for offences under Sections 376, 420, 504, and 506 of the IPC.
appellant_arguments: The complainant was fully aware that the appellant was already married and had two wives, which negates any allegation of being cheated or induced by a false promise of marriage.

The allegations made against the accused do not constitute the offences alleged, or the evidence adduced manifestly fails to prove the charge, warranting the exercise of the High Court's inherent jurisdiction to quash the proceedings.
respondent_arguments: The State-respondent contested the appeal, although they did not file a counter-affidavit. The complainant (Respondent no. 2) did not appear to contest the matter despite being served notice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The High Court's inherent jurisdiction can be exercised to quash proceedings where, although the allegations constitute an offence, there is either no legal evidence adduced in support of the case, or the evidence provided manifestly and clearly fails to prove the charge. This power is distinct from the function of a trial court and does not involve an inquiry into the reliability of existing evidence.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In the opinion of the court, allowing the criminal proceeding against the appellant to continue where no criminal liability can be attached would amount to an abuse of the process of court. Based on the facts and circumstances, the court was satisfied that the appellant was entitled to the relief of quashing the complaint/FIR.
legal_tests_applied: The court's power to quash criminal proceedings under Section 482 of the CrPC should be exercised to prevent the abuse of the process of any court or otherwise to secure the ends of justice. This power can be invoked in specific exceptional cases, such as where the allegations and evidence manifestly fail to prove the charge, as established in R.P. Kapur v. State of Punjab and reiterated in Neeharika Infrastructure Private Limited v. State of Maharashtra & Ors.
policy_considerations: Every case involving human relationships and psychology must be decided on its own peculiar facts and circumstances, as these matters are dynamic and permeated with unpredictable emotions and sensitivities.
Quashing a criminal FIR does not necessarily bar the complainant from seeking other remedies available under the law.

The inherent jurisdiction of the High Court under Section 482 CrPC is intended to prevent the abuse of the process of court, such as the continuation of a criminal proceeding where no criminal liability can be attached.
